title: Autonomous heredity in a chemically distinct genetic polymer

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a hereditary system whose information is carried by a genetic polymer chemically distinct from DNA and RNA, and which repeatedly copies that information while regenerating its essential replication catalyst. Success would require more than producing an alternative polymer: inherited sequences would sustain the machinery needed for subsequent generations, and sequence changes could produce functional differences that are themselves inherited.

TNA is one candidate alternative genetic polymer. Maola and colleagues demonstrated its synthesis using an engineered protein polymerase, but the reviewed methods retain DNA templates, bacterial production of the protein catalyst, and laboratory selection and recovery procedures. Those dependencies illustrate the gap between making an alternative genetic polymer and establishing autonomous heredity in it.

Scope synthesis: autonomy here concerns hereditary continuity and regeneration of essential replication machinery. It need not include autonomous metabolism, a cellular enclosure, production of all raw materials, or independence from supplied substrates and energy. The concept also does not require the alternative polymer to have an entirely unrelated molecular architecture; a substantially different genetic backbone is sufficient to pose the central scientific question.

significance.text: Conditional significance: an independently evolving hereditary system based on a substantially different genetic backbone would demonstrate that sustained biochemical heredity can operate beyond familiar DNA/RNA backbone chemistry. Its strongest direct consequence would be experimental evidence that information copying, inherited function and regeneration of replication machinery can form a continuing system in another polymer chemistry.

This would extend the scientific meaning of alternative-polymer synthesis. The Maola result establishes an engineered route for producing TNA; the proposed advance would connect alternative-polymer information to the continuing production of the machinery responsible for its inheritance. It would therefore address a different capability from improved polymerase performance or externally directed selection alone.

The reviewed Maola abstract describes TNA as resistant to nucleases and acid-mediated degradation, properties that motivate interest in alternative genetic materials. Conditional downstream possibilities include more durable functional molecules for medicine or materials. Autonomous heredity would not by itself establish useful therapeutic activity, safety, manufacturability or a practical materials application; each would require separate development.

Interpretive limit: such a demonstration would not alone establish autonomous cellular life, explain how life originated on Earth, or prove that arbitrary polymer chemistries can support heredity. It would establish a particular working alternative within the chemical conditions and functional range actually demonstrated.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is a continuing hereditary cycle in which a chemically distinct polymer carries sequence information, that information is copied, and the essential replication catalyst is regenerated under the control of the inherited program. In the reviewed TNA work, synthesis and selection instead depend on an externally supplied protein enzyme and DNA-based laboratory workflows. Closing that hereditary cycle is the central missing step relative to this example; the supplied evidence does not establish a field-wide absence of such systems.

Engineering synthesis: the system must connect inherited sequence to replication activity. A catalyst made from the alternative polymer would need both useful catalytic function and reliable copying of the sequences that regenerate it. If the catalyst were a protein, the system would need a demonstrated way for the alternative hereditary program to direct its production and renewal. Supplying fresh enzyme from an external bacterial expression workflow would leave that essential dependency outside the hereditary cycle.

Engineering synthesis: copying must preserve enough sequence information to maintain function across generations while permitting heritable variation and selection. Concrete barriers include copying functionally useful sequences without prohibitive errors or sequence bias, completing repeated copying cycles, and maintaining compatible conditions for polymer synthesis, catalyst activity and product reuse. Catalyst regeneration must also keep pace with dilution and degradation. These are requirements inferred from the proposed capability, not measurements established by the supplied studies.

The reviewed Maola methods identify specific dependencies that a convincing autonomous system would need to replace or place outside the hereditary program: DNA-templated TNA synthesis, reverse transcription of products into cDNA, PCR, bacterial expression and externally managed library recovery. These procedures are effective tools for enzyme engineering, but they do not themselves demonstrate inheritance carried continuously by TNA.

current_state.text: On 1 October 2024, Maola and colleagues published an engineered protein polymerase for TNA synthesis, identified in the reviewed abstract as polymerase 10–92. The abstract and supplementary methods support a component-level achievement: an engineered enzyme can synthesize an alternative genetic polymer. They do not establish autonomous TNA heredity or internal regeneration of the essential replication catalyst.

The reviewed supplementary methods describe synthesis across DNA templates, bacterial expression and purification of the protein polymerase, externally managed selection, recovery of plasmid DNA, PCR and library regeneration. The fidelity workflow also purifies a synthesis product and reverse transcribes it into cDNA. Thus the reported directed evolution improves a protein catalyst through a DNA/protein laboratory system; it is not evidence that TNA independently carries and renews that system's hereditary program.

The supplied research attributes to Taylor and colleagues a 1 December 2014 report of catalysts made from four synthetic genetic-polymer backbones, including a synthetic-polymer ligase, with polymerases and DNA intermediates used during selection and copying. Those historical details remain unverified in this record: the supplied PubMed artifact contained only a cookie challenge, exposing neither the paper's scientific text nor the cited Extended Data Figure 1 description. This access limitation does not establish that the reported results are false.

Access to the Maola study was substantial but incomplete. The supplied review examined a subscription-preview article page and supplementary material, including text covering the full retained 51-page methods supplement. Figure images were not inspected through that text extraction, and the complete main article was absent. The record does not substantiate the earlier assertion that a main-article PDF request redirected to the article page.

Temporal limitation: the supplied record contains no bounded freshness search. It supports the dated Maola achievement and its documented dependencies, but cannot establish whether autonomous alternative-polymer heredity remained unachieved as of 1 November 2026 or at the later source-retrieval date. The concept therefore remains a proposed capability here without a claim that the supplied examples exhaust the field.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a non-DNA/non-RNA genetic polymer should sustain repeated, sequence-dependent replication and heritable functional adaptation, with its essential replication catalyst encoded and regenerated within the system. The experiment should connect inherited sequence, catalyst renewal and subsequent replication, rather than demonstrate these functions only in separate preparations. This is a proposed criterion, not an established consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Alternative-polymer heredity integrates replication, adaptation and encoded catalyst regeneration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed continuity test: serial transfer or an equivalent continuing experiment should run long enough, with sufficient dilution and measured catalyst turnover, to exclude persistence of the initially supplied catalyst as the explanation for replication. Investigators should specify generation counts, transfer conditions and catalyst measurements in advance. No universal numerical threshold is supplied here; the necessary duration depends on catalyst stability, dilution and the design of the system.
completion_criteria.label: Continued replication excludes persistence of the initially supplied catalyst

completion_criteria.text: Proposed inheritance test: sequence changes should produce measurable functional differences that persist through subsequent replication, with adaptation linked to the inherited alternative-polymer sequence. Controls should establish that DNA or RNA contamination, hidden intermediates or an external DNA/RNA program are not carrying the hereditary information. These controls address a concrete distinction from the DNA templates and cDNA recovery documented in the reviewed TNA study.
completion_criteria.label: Inherited alternative-polymer sequences determine functional adaptation without DNA/RNA heredity

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries: independent preparations and independent laboratories should reproduce the core hereditary cycle using disclosed sequences, reagents, feed conditions and analysis methods. Reports should identify supplied substrates and energy, environmental tolerances, sequence-dependent failures and any externally performed operations. Tests across multiple sequences and conditions would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not literal universality or independence from every external resource.
completion_criteria.label: Independent laboratories reproduce hereditary cycles with disclosed methods and boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BCH-04, “A chemically plausible route from simple feedstocks to evolving heredity,” overlaps in the emergence of sustained inheritance and evolution. Its central requirement is a plausible chemical route from simple starting materials. BCH-07 instead tests whether heredity can operate in a distinct genetic-polymer chemistry and may begin with sophisticated synthetic monomers, purified catalysts and supplied energy. Neither achievement automatically establishes the other.

Roster-based synthesis: BCH-03, “A self-maintaining, evolvable cell assembled from defined components,” shares the requirements for regeneration and sustained evolution, but adds cellular organization and broader self-maintenance. BCH-07 could be demonstrated in a cell-free system with externally supplied substrates; a self-maintaining cell using ordinary DNA/RNA would not by itself satisfy BCH-07.

Roster-based synthesis: BCH-01, “General design of enzymes for new chemical reactions,” could contribute catalysts for alternative-polymer synthesis or regeneration. BCH-02, “Predict biochemical function from molecular sequence and environment,” could help connect alternative-polymer sequences to activity and operating conditions. Enzyme design and function prediction are enabling capabilities; neither alone demonstrates a continuing hereditary cycle.

Roster-based synthesis: BCH-05, comprehensive single-cell proteoform reading; BCH-06, a multiplexed biochemical flight recorder; BCH-08, resolving the nitrogenase reaction cycle; BCH-09, predicting and controlling condensate organization; BCH-10, predicting modification-dependent biochemical networks; and BCH-11, structural reading of complex glycans retain distinct measurement, mechanistic or control objectives. The supplied material establishes no direct dependency between those objectives and alternative-polymer heredity.

unresolved_issues: The supplied Taylor artifact does not permit verification of the four-backbone catalysis, synthetic-polymer ligase or DNA-mediated selection and copying claims.

The complete Maola main article was not supplied, and supplementary figure images were not inspected through the text extraction; conclusions here remain bounded by the reviewed abstract and supplementary text.
No supplied freshness search establishes whether autonomous heredity in an alternative genetic polymer remained unachieved as of 1 November 2026 or the later retrieval date.

A concrete experimental specification must define sufficient generations, catalyst turnover, dilution, sequence diversity and functional inheritance to exclude persistence of initially supplied machinery.
The proposed system's catalyst chemistry, regeneration pathway and acceptable external support remain unspecified; those choices determine the engineering burden and demonstrated scope of autonomy.

brief.title: Heredity built from different genetic material
possible: Scientists could study inheritance in genetic material chemically different from DNA and RNA, the familiar molecules that carry genetic instructions. This material would pass information through repeated generations and renew the molecules that drive its copying.
Changes in its inherited instructions could produce lasting changes in what the system does. Researchers could study a continuing system that evolves using a different kind of molecular chain.
why: This would demonstrate that sustained biochemical inheritance can work beyond DNA and RNA chemistry. It would connect copying, inherited function and renewal of the copying machinery in a working alternative.
Such research could also contribute to more durable functional molecules for medicine or materials. Some alternative genetic materials already resist chemical and biological breakdown.

sources.who: Alexander I. Taylor, Philipp Holliger and colleagues
sources.showed: They made catalysts, molecules that speed chemical reactions, from alternative genetic materials. These cut or joined RNA, and one joined pieces of an alternative genetic material.
sources.quote: We also describe an XNA-XNA ligase metalloenzyme in the FANA framework, establishing catalysis in an entirely synthetic system and enabling the synthesis of FANA oligomers and an active RNA endonuclease FANAzyme from its constituent parts.
sources.cited_for: Alternative genetic materials can perform chemical reactions needed for functional molecular systems.
sources.not_established: These reactions did not establish a continuing hereditary system that renews its essential copying catalyst.

sources.who: Victoria A. Maola, Eric J. Yik, John C. Chaput and colleagues
sources.showed: They engineered a protein enzyme, a biological catalyst, to make TNA, an artificial genetic material. Their process still used DNA templates and protein production in bacteria.
sources.quote: A crystal structure of the closed ternary complex reveals the degree of structural change required to remodel the active site pocket for improved TNA synthesis activity.
sources.cited_for: Engineered proteins can make alternative genetic material, providing a component needed for a different hereditary system.
sources.not_established: TNA did not direct the renewal of its copying enzyme or sustain its own hereditary cycle.

shown: Taylor and colleagues made alternative genetic materials that act as catalysts, including one that joins pieces of such material. Maola and colleagues engineered a protein enzyme that makes TNA.
These achievements supply useful parts. In the TNA work, DNA templates, bacteria and laboratory procedures still supplied the copying machinery and managed its improvement.
missing: A continuing cycle must link inherited alternative genetic instructions to renewal of the catalyst that copies them.
Copying must preserve useful instructions across generations while allowing inherited changes in function.
Replication must continue after the initially supplied catalyst has disappeared, under conditions that also allow catalyst renewal and reuse of copied material.

milestones.label: Alternative genetic material sustains inheritance and renews copying machinery
milestones.explanation: A system would have to combine repeated copying, inherited functional adaptation and catalyst renewal directed by its alternative genetic instructions. This would connect the essential parts into a continuing hereditary cycle.

milestones.label: Copying continues after the starting catalyst disappears
milestones.explanation: Repeated transfers or an equivalent experiment would have to demonstrate copying after dilution and measured catalyst replacement exclude the starting supply. This would establish that renewed machinery sustains the cycle.

milestones.label: Alternative genetic instructions determine inherited changes in function
milestones.explanation: Sequence changes would have to cause functional differences that persist through copying, with controls excluding DNA or RNA as the hereditary carrier. This would locate adaptation in the alternative genetic material.

milestones.label: Independent laboratories reproduce the hereditary cycle
milestones.explanation: Independent laboratories would have to reproduce the cycle using disclosed methods and test different sequences and conditions. This would establish reliability and define its dependence on supplied materials and outside operations.

uncertain: The required number of generations depends on how long the catalyst lasts, how strongly it is diluted and how its replacement is measured.
The catalyst's chemistry and the route by which inherited instructions renew it remain unspecified.
The system could receive raw materials and energy; the acceptable extent of other external support still needs definition.

page.title: Autonomous heredity in xeno nucleic acids
page.definition: A xeno nucleic acid (XNA), a synthetic genetic polymer with a backbone different from DNA and RNA, carries information through repeated copying and regenerates its essential replication catalyst. Sequence variation produces inherited functional differences that affect reproductive success.

goal.need: All known life depends on two genetic polymers, DNA and RNA. Laboratory selection can preserve an XNA function by copying its sequence back into DNA, leaving open whether that backbone can sustain evolution independently. An independently evolving XNA lineage would give origin-of-life biology a second experimental model of heredity and broaden the genetic chemistries considered in searches for life elsewhere. Whether such a chemistry occurs in nature would remain an observational question.

statements.body: Belgian Scientific Institute of Public Health, Biosafety and Biotechnology Unit
statements.quote: the XNA must be able to catalyze its own replication (i.e. to undergo evolution on a self-sustained manner).
statements.context: Section 3.4 identifies this requirement for building new genetic systems based on XNAs.

statements.body: National Research Council, The Limits of Organic Life in Planetary Systems

completion.title: XNA heredity sustains copying, replication-catalyst renewal and Darwinian evolution.
completion.criterion: Serial propagation of an XNA population maintains sequence-dependent copying and heritable variation with differential reproductive success. Inherited XNA regenerates the essential replication catalyst, and copying persists beyond experimentally measured carry-over of the starting catalyst. Substrates and energy may be supplied; DNA or RNA must not carry the hereditary programme. This is an Atlas operational criterion, not an externally adopted acceptance protocol.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas, interpreting the Belgian biosafety report’s qualitative XNA goal and published definitions of nucleic-acid self-replication.
completion.basis: The Belgian report describes self-sustained evolution qualitatively. The Atlas criterion requires evidence for both renewal of the copying activity and selection among inherited variants. A six-unit peptide nucleic acid accelerated formation of copies of its own sequence. That observation establishes autocatalysis for the tested sequence and leaves the inheritance and selection of variants untested.

milestones.title: Sequence information survives a complete DNA-to-XNA-to-DNA copying cycle.
milestones.criterion: A defined DNA sequence is copied into XNA, and that XNA serves as the template for complementary DNA synthesis. Sequence analysis of the recovered DNA establishes information transfer across the complete cycle. Supplied protein enzymes are allowed.
milestones.set_by: Published XNA copying and fidelity assays of Pinheiro and colleagues, Taylor and Holliger, and Wang and colleagues.
milestones.threshold_quote: FANA replication fidelity was measured by sequencing a DNA template that was transcribed into FANA and reverse transcribed back into cDNA.

milestones.title: An XNA catalyst assembles an active XNA enzyme from XNA fragments.
milestones.criterion: An XNA catalyst joins XNA fragments. An activity assay shows that the assembled XNA product itself catalyses a reaction.
milestones.set_by: XNA catalysis research convention, exemplified by Taylor et al.’s FANA enzyme-assembly experiment and subsequent X-SELEX protocol; the assembly test was demonstrated specifically for FANA.
milestones.threshold_quote: enabling the synthesis of FANA oligomers and an active RNA endonuclease FANAzyme from its constituent parts.

milestones.title: An XNA template directs full-length synthesis of an XNA extension of the same chemistry.
milestones.criterion: A supplied polymerase extends a primer to the end of an XNA template. The entire newly synthesized segment has the same backbone chemistry as the template, and copying proceeds without an intervening DNA or RNA template. The primer may have a different chemistry.
milestones.set_by: Zhang and colleagues, Figure 6, primer-extension assay on a 2′-fluoro-RNA template.
milestones.threshold_quote: Synthesis of DNA, RNA, 2′-F-RNA, and FANA using a 2′-F-RNA template 2′-F-T34 by F762A.

milestones.title: An XNA hereditary programme regenerates an active replication catalyst for a subsequent copying reaction.
milestones.criterion: One XNA-directed cycle produces a new copy of the essential replication catalyst. A subsequent copying reaction demonstrates the activity of the newly produced catalyst. The catalyst may be XNA or a product encoded by the inherited XNA. External DNA or RNA expression of the replacement catalyst does not qualify.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; no outside XNA-specific catalyst-renewal test was found. MRC’s published RNA self-replication definition supplies a limited precedent, not an XNA threshold.

milestones.title: Selection yields an XNA sequence that binds a specified target with measurable affinity and specificity.
milestones.criterion: Selection from a population of different XNA sequences enriches a target-binding sequence. Binding measurements on the selected XNA establish its affinity for the target and its ability to discriminate that target from a control. DNA intermediates and supplied copying enzymes are allowed.
milestones.set_by: The aptamer selection and binding assays of Pinheiro and colleagues.
milestones.threshold_quote: bind their targets with high affinity and specificity

not_found: No published minimum generation count, dilution factor or copying fidelity was found for autonomous XNA heredity.
No academy or biosafety-body statement was found disputing the value or feasibility of autonomous XNA heredity specifically.
No published XNA population was found that both renewed its essential replication catalyst and sustained selection among inherited sequence variants.

goal.need = "All known life depends on two genetic polymers, DNA and RNA. Laboratory selection can preserve an XNA function by copying its sequence back into DNA, leaving open whether that backbone can sustain evolution independently. An independently evolving XNA lineage would give origin-of-life biology a second experimental model of heredity and broaden the genetic chemistries considered in searches for life elsewhere. Whether such a chemistry occurs in nature would remain an observational question.". Reason: The present rationale gives dates and polymerase performance figures but leaves the consequence for interpreting terrestrial and extraterrestrial heredity unexplained.

add statement by National Research Council, The Limits of Organic Life in Planetary Systems, 2007: "molecular systems capable of Darwinian evolution that are different from standard DNA and RNA". Reason: The National Research Council explicitly recommended laboratory studies of Darwinian evolution with alternative genetic chemistry.

edit completion: basis = "The Belgian report describes self-sustained evolution qualitatively. The Atlas criterion requires evidence for both renewal of the copying activity and selection among inherited variants. A six-unit peptide nucleic acid accelerated formation of copies of its own sequence. That observation establishes autocatalysis for the tested sequence and leaves the inheritance and selection of variants untested."; refs = [4, 6, 7, 15]. Reason: The peptide nucleic acid experiment supplies a published example that distinguishes making more of one sequence from sustaining selection among variants.
add case "Arabino nucleic acid". Reason: Pinheiro and colleagues measured information transfer through arabino nucleic acid separately from its 2′-fluoro derivative.
add case "Locked nucleic acid". Reason: Locked nucleic acid was a distinct backbone in the six-chemistry copying experiment and has its own measured round-trip error rate.
add case "Peptide nucleic acid". Reason: Peptide nucleic acid has a published autocatalytic copying result directly relevant to the distinction between replication and evolution.

edit m1: criterion = "A defined DNA sequence is copied into XNA, and that XNA serves as the template for complementary DNA synthesis. Sequence analysis of the recovered DNA establishes information transfer across the complete cycle. Supplied protein enzymes are allowed."; set_by = "Published XNA copying and fidelity assays of Pinheiro and colleagues, Taylor and Holliger, and Wang and colleagues."; set_by_kind = "protocol"; threshold_quote = "FANA replication fidelity was measured by sequencing a DNA template that was transcribed into FANA and reverse transcribed back into cDNA."; threshold_ref = 11; refs = [1, 3, 8, 9, 11, 16]. Reason: Maola and colleagues sequenced the product of a complete DNA-to-TNA-to-DNA cycle, so the current criterion understates the evidence attached to m1.

add milestone after m1: "Selection yields an XNA sequence that binds a specified target with measurable affinity and specificity.". Reason: The current milestones cover sequence recovery and enzyme assembly but omit the demonstrated selection of an inherited XNA binding function.

edit m2: criterion = "An XNA catalyst joins XNA fragments. An activity assay shows that the assembled XNA product itself catalyses a reaction."; threshold_quote = "enabling the synthesis of FANA oligomers and an active RNA endonuclease FANAzyme from its constituent parts."; threshold_ref = 2. Reason: The m2 criterion mixes the enzyme-assembly test with the FANA outcome and a survey of other backbones.

edit m3: criterion = "A supplied polymerase extends a primer to the end of an XNA template. The entire newly synthesized segment has the same backbone chemistry as the template, and copying proceeds without an intervening DNA or RNA template. The primer may have a different chemistry."; set_by = "Zhang and colleagues, Figure 6, primer-extension assay on a 2\u2032-fluoro-RNA template."; threshold_quote = "Synthesis of DNA, RNA, 2\u2032-F-RNA, and FANA using a 2\u2032-F-RNA template 2\u2032-F-T34 by F762A."; threshold_ref = 9; refs = [1, 9]. Reason: Zhang’s template and primer lengths describe one assay, and Pinheiro and colleagues also reported direct FANA-templated FANA synthesis in supplementary figure S9.

edit m4: criterion = "One XNA-directed cycle produces a new copy of the essential replication catalyst. A subsequent copying reaction demonstrates the activity of the newly produced catalyst. The catalyst may be XNA or a product encoded by the inherited XNA. External DNA or RNA expression of the replacement catalyst does not qualify.". Reason: The final sentence of m4 is a search verdict that can become outdated independently of the catalyst-renewal test.

remove not found 1. Reason: Chapter 1 of Victoria Maola Gross’s dissertation reprints the article, identifies three reaction replicates for the rate measurement and reports fidelity across the complete copying cycle.

add not found: "No academy or biosafety-body statement was found disputing the value or feasibility of autonomous XNA heredity specifically.". Reason: The standing-body question needs a search result specific to autonomous XNA heredity.

add not found: "No published XNA population was found that both renewed its essential replication catalyst and sustained selection among inherited sequence variants.". Reason: The existing search note concerns numerical thresholds and leaves the status of the combined completion test unstated.
remove statement 1. Reason: The 2023 lecture describes published selections of XNA ligands and catalysts, and its forward-looking self-replication example concerns RNA.
